Theory Session 1

From Program to Process to Thread

Motivating Scenario

A cyber dashboard cannot do one thing at a time

Before definitions, predict the problem

Ask StudentsA security tool is scanning a huge log file. The same execution path also updates the interface. What might happen?Tap to reveal
Suggested Answer

The interface may freeze or respond slowly. A separate thread can let scanning continue while the interface remains responsive.

Core Terminology

Program, process and thread are different ideas

📄

Program

Code stored on disk. It is passive until executed.

📦

Process

A running program with memory, files, resources and execution context.

🧵

Thread

A lightweight execution path inside a process.

Analogy: program = recipe; process = kitchen in operation; threads = cooks working inside that kitchen.
Visual Model

One process can contain many threads

📦

Process

Own memory + resources

T1T2T3
→
🧠

Shared inside process

Threads commonly share code, heap memory, and open resources. Each has its own execution path.

Single vs Multithreaded Program

Same application, different execution organization

Single-threaded

One path handles tasks one by one.

T1ABCD

Multithreaded

Several paths can make progress.

T1AT2BT3C
Click Run Visual to discuss task progress.
Why Use Threads?

Threads help when work can overlap safely

⚡

Responsiveness

Keep UI active while work continues.

🧮

CPU Work

Use multiple cores for independent computation.

🌐

I/O Overlap

Wait for network or disk while other work proceeds.

📈

Throughput

Handle more jobs per unit time.

Multicore Connection

Threads expose work that hardware can schedule

Key idea

A multicore processor provides multiple execution resources.

Threads provide schedulable units of work.

Caution: more threads do not automatically mean more speed.
Quick Recap

Concurrency organizes work. Parallelism executes work simultaneously.

🔀

Concurrency

Multiple tasks make progress during overlapping time periods. This may happen through switching.

⚡

Parallelism

Multiple tasks execute at the same instant using multiple processing resources.

Multithreading can support concurrency and parallelism depending on hardware, scheduling, and workload.
Thread Lifecycle

A thread changes state during execution

Why this matters

  • A created thread may not run immediately.
  • A running thread may become blocked.
  • A waiting thread may return to runnable state.
  • A terminated thread has finished.

Foreground and Background Threads

Thread type can affect application lifetime

TypeSimple meaningCybersecurity example
Foreground ThreadKeeps the application alive until it finishes.Main monitoring service receiving security events.
Background ThreadSupports work and may stop when foreground work ends.Cache cleanup, telemetry upload, optional report refresh.
Important: foreground/background is about application lifetime, not task importance.

Short Conceptual Code

A thread starts another execution path

// Conceptual C# fragment
Thread t = new Thread(ScanLogs);
t.Start();

Console.WriteLine("Main continues...");

void ScanLogs() {
    // long-running analysis
}

Instructor explanation

  • Main continues its own execution path.
  • t runs ScanLogs separately.
  • The runtime and OS control exact scheduling.
This is a concept demo, not a lab task.
Session 1 Checkpoint

Confirm the foundation

Question 1What is the difference between a process and a thread?Tap to reveal
Answer

A process is a running program with resources. A thread is an execution path inside that process.

Question 2Why might a thread enter waiting state?Tap to reveal
Answer

It may wait for I/O, a lock, another thread, a resource, sleep time, or an event.

Theory Session 2

Coordination, Race Conditions and IPC

🧨

Shared State

Understand what can go wrong when threads share data.

🛡️

Synchronization

See why locks, mutexes and semaphores exist.

📨

IPC

Understand controlled communication between processes.

Last session: multiple execution paths. Now: how do we coordinate them correctly?
Shared Data

Threads are useful, but shared data can be dangerous

Shared examples

  • Total alerts detected.
  • Packet queue.
  • Connection counter.
  • Threat-score table.

Possible errors

  • Lost update.
  • Corrupted state.
  • Inconsistent read.
  • Timing-dependent behavior.
When correctness depends on timing, the program becomes hard to trust.
Race Condition

A race condition makes output depend on execution timing

👀

Read

Two threads read the same old value.

🧮

Compute

Each computes a new value privately.

✍️

Write

One update overwrites another.

Definition: a race condition occurs when program correctness depends on uncontrolled ordering of concurrent operations.
Interactive Execution Trace

Two threads increment one counter

Shared Counter

10

Trace Explanation

Expected final value after two increments is 12.
Think → Predict

Why can the final value be wrong?

Ask StudentsIf two threads both increment counter = 10, why might the final value become 11 instead of 12?Tap to reveal
Suggested Answer

Both may read 10 before either writes. Each computes 11. The second write overwrites the first update, so one increment is lost.

Critical Section

Protect the part that touches shared mutable data

🔓EnterRequest permission.
📍Critical SectionAccess shared data.
🔐ProtectPrevent unsafe overlap.
🚪ExitRelease permission.
Example: incrementing a shared alert counter is a critical section when many threads can update it.
Synchronization Intuition

Locks, mutexes and semaphores coordinate access

🔒

Lock / Mutex

Usually allows one thread at a time to access a protected section.

🚦

Semaphore

Controls access to a limited number of identical resources.

📣

Signal / Event

Lets one thread notify another that something happened.

Synchronization improves correctness, but too much waiting can reduce performance.
Conceptual Pseudocode

Protect the update, not the whole program

lock(counterLock)
    temp = counter
    temp = temp + 1
    counter = temp
unlock(counterLock)

How to explain

  • Only one thread enters this block at a time.
  • The read-compute-write sequence is protected.
  • The protected region should remain small.

Inter-Process Communication

Threads share a process. Processes are separated.

🧵

Threads

Can share memory inside the same process. Fast, but synchronization is needed.

📦

Processes

Usually have separate memory spaces. They need IPC to communicate.

IPC Visual Model

Processes communicate through controlled channels

📦

Process A

Own memory space

⇄
📨

IPC Channel

Pipe · Socket · Queue · Shared memory · Signal

IPC is important in security tools because collectors, analyzers, dashboards and services may run separately.

Why Thread Pools?

Creating a new thread for every tiny task can be expensive

♻️

Reuse

Existing worker threads handle many tasks over time.

🎛️

Control

The system can limit how many threads run.

📈

Throughput

Useful for many independent small jobs.

Design Reasoning

Which mechanism fits the situation?

SituationLikely direction
Need low-overhead shared stateUse threads, with synchronization for shared mutable data.
Need isolation or fault containmentUse separate processes or services.
Need communication between processesUse IPC or network messaging.
Many short independent jobsUse a thread pool or task scheduler abstraction.
Common Misconceptions

Correct these ideas early

Incorrect idea

  • More threads always make programs faster.
  • Threads and processes are the same.
  • Race conditions are easy to reproduce.
  • IPC is only for distributed systems.

Correct idea

  • Threads add overhead and coordination cost.
  • Processes isolate resources; threads share resources.
  • Race conditions may appear only sometimes.
  • IPC can also happen on the same machine.

Exit Check

Four quick checks

Q1Process vs thread?

Process = running program with resources. Thread = execution path inside a process.

Q2Race condition?

A correctness error caused by uncontrolled ordering/timing of concurrent operations.

Q3Why IPC?

Separate processes need controlled mechanisms to exchange data or signals.

Q4Why thread pool?

It reuses workers and controls overhead for many independent tasks.
